title: Narrow bridges are choking about 80 rivers, Prothom Alo finds
excerpt: About 290 bridges and culverts are harming some 80 rivers and canals in 26 districts, a Prothom Alo investigation finds, with LGED the largest builder.

image.alt: A narrow stretch of the Gondor river with an eroded bank in Bangladesh
image.credit: Anup Sadi / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content:
About 290 bridges and culverts are harming roughly 80 rivers and canals in 26 districts, and many more are not recorded, according to an investigation by Mostafa Yusuf published in Prothom Alo on 17 November.

The report draws on an incomplete Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB) list obtained under the Right to Information Act, data from the National River Conservation Commission and interviews. It says approach roads and embankments fill river land and narrow channels, causing silt to build up upstream and banks to erode downstream, while low bridges block boats.

The Local Government Engineering Department (LGED) is the largest builder of the harmful structures, with 97 bridges and 24 culverts, the report says. The Disaster Management and Relief Ministry follows with 45 bridges and 45 culverts, and the Roads and Highways Department with 24 bridges and 3 culverts. In about 90% of the 153 structures it commented on, BWDB recommended lengthening the bridge to match the river's width.

At the Salehpur Bridge over the Turag in Savar, a fisherman told the paper: "The bridge is killing the river." The Khakdon in Barguna has 21 bridges along 17 km.

LGED's bridge design head told the paper that LGED has studied bridges under 100 m since 2005. An unnamed senior LGED official said political pressure had led to some short bridges being built.

Why it matters

Narrowed rivers drain more slowly, which can worsen waterlogging and flooding and damage fisheries and river transport. NGOs working on disaster risk reduction, water and livelihoods in affected districts can use the findings in local risk assessments and in advocacy with upazila and union councils, which also build culverts. The report notes that some NGOs and private parties have built such structures too.

What to watch

  • Whether LGED and other agencies commit to lengthening or replacing the worst structures.
  • Whether the River Conservation Commission takes up the findings.

Sources

  • Prothom Alo (Bangla), 17 Nov 2026
